title: Home with the texts
hookLine: Xuanzang comes home with the texts and spends his life translating; centuries later he becomes the monk in Journey to the West

lines: A MONKEY, A PIG, A RIVER GIANT.
A MONK ON A WHITE HORSE.
cards: A monkey who can somersault across the sky. A pig with a rake and a big appetite. A quiet giant from a river.

And in the middle of them, riding a white horse, a gentle monk heading west for scriptures. If you've seen a cartoon, a TV series or a video game about the Monkey King, you've met Xuanzang, or a version of him.
The real monk walked home with his texts. The legend gave him a monkey. Today, both.

teach.b: First, the homecoming. Xuanzang had left China against a ban.
He came back with horses loaded with Buddhist texts in Sanskrit, along with images and relics, and his biography describes crowds lining the way into the capital.

The emperor, instead of punishing him, received him and asked him to write down everything he had seen in the western lands. That book still exists; its English translator called it Buddhist Records of the Western World.
Second, the rest of his life. Xuanzang spent his remaining years translating with teams of monks, turning what he had carried home into Chinese.
A version of the short Heart Sutra still chanted in Chinese is traditionally credited to him. The desert crossing was one journey.

teach.h: TRANSLATING FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE.
teach.b: The translating took the rest of his life. Third, the legend.

teach.h: A NOVEL: JOURNEY TO THE WEST.
teach.b: Long after his death, storytellers kept his journey going, and it grew into a long novel, Journey to the West.

In it the monk is called Tripitaka, and he's protected on the road by a band of strange disciples: Monkey, born from a stone, clever and impossible to control; Pigsy; Sandy; and a dragon who has become his horse.
Fourth, what the monkey might mean.

teach.h: THE RESTLESS MIND, THE STEADY PURPOSE.
teach.b: Some readers see Monkey as the restless mind, brilliant, quick, always leaping off somewhere, and the monk as the steady purpose that keeps the whole party walking west.
Whatever the novel intends, the pair is easy to spot in any busy day: the leaping thought, and the slow walk forward.

how: Xuanzang's translations are still read in Chinese Buddhist communities, and Journey to the West is retold in operas, films and comics.

practice: Bring to mind a journey of your own: a real trip, a move, an illness, a hard year. Find one moment on that road when you almost turned back, and one thing you carried home from it.
If your mind starts leaping like the monkey, smile at it, and come back to the road.

wordCard.voice: Tripitaka. The three baskets of the Buddhist canon, and the name the novel gives the monk who carried them home.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the three baskets, a name for the whole Buddhist canon, and the monk's name in the novel.

carryVoice: Your line: the monkey and the monk. A real walk home, and a legend that kept on walking. Day nine hundred nine, done.
